Kummer's Test

One big frame unifies several convergence tests in this scene. A single auxiliary sequence switches which test you get.

Weight the ratio to build a new quantity. The sign of that quantity decides convergence or divergence. Set every weight to 1 and you get the ratio test. Set the weights to the term index and you get Raabe's test. The precise formulas are below.

For example, turn a dial on a ⚙️ machine and the inspection strength changes. One position gives a weak check, another position a strong one. The auxiliary sequence is that dial.

Kn:=pnanan+1−pn+1≥c>0 ⇒ ∑an convergesK_n := p_n\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - p_{n+1} \ge c > 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \sum a_n\ \text{converges}Kn​:=pn​an+1​an​​−pn+1​≥c>0 ⇒ ∑an​ converges
Kn≤0, ∑1pn=∞ ⇒ ∑an divergesK_n \le 0,\ \sum\frac{1}{p_n} = \infty \ \Rightarrow\ \sum a_n\ \text{diverges}Kn​≤0, ∑pn​1​=∞ ⇒ ∑an​ diverges

(ii) If Kn≤0K_n \le 0Kn​≤0 eventually and ∑1pn\sum \frac{1}{p_n}∑pn​1​ diverges, then ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ diverges.

Show that Raabe's test is Kummer's test with pn=np_n = npn​=n, and prove that for L:=lim⁡n→∞n(anan+1−1)L := \lim_{n\to\infty} n\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right)L:=limn→∞​n(an+1​an​​−1): convergence if L>1L > 1L>1, divergence if L<1L < 1L<1.

pn=n:Kn=n(anan+1−1)−1  →n→∞  L−1p_n = n: \qquad K_n = n\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right) - 1 \;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\; L - 1pn​=n:Kn​=n(an+1​an​​−1)−1n→∞​L−1
Show proof

  1. Plugging in pn=np_n = npn​=n gives Kn=nanan+1−(n+1)=n(anan+1−1)−1K_n = n \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - (n+1) = n\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right) - 1Kn​=nan+1​an​​−(n+1)=n(an+1​an​​−1)−1. Taking limits, Kn→L−1K_n \to L - 1Kn​→L−1 — the Raabe quotient shifted by 1.

  2. If L>1L > 1L>1, then Kn→L−1>0K_n \to L - 1 > 0Kn​→L−1>0, so eventually Kn≥L−12>0K_n \ge \frac{L-1}{2} > 0Kn​≥2L−1​>0. Kummer's convergent half (with c=L−12c = \frac{L-1}{2}c=2L−1​) gives convergence of ∑an\sum a_n∑an​.

  3. If L<1L < 1L<1, then Kn→L−1<0K_n \to L - 1 < 0Kn​→L−1<0, so eventually Kn≤L−12<0K_n \le \frac{L-1}{2} < 0Kn​≤2L−1​<0. And ∑1pn=∑1n\sum \frac{1}{p_n} = \sum \frac{1}{n}∑pn​1​=∑n1​ diverges (harmonic series), so Kummer's divergent half gives divergence of ∑an\sum a_n∑an​.

Numerical check (Gauss example a=2a = 2a=2): anan+1=1+2n+1\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} = 1 + \frac{2}{n+1}an+1​an​​=1+n+12​, so n(anan+1−1)=2nn+1→2=Ln\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right) = \frac{2n}{n+1} \to 2 = Ln(an+1​an​​−1)=n+12n​→2=L and Kn=2nn+1−1=n−1n+1→1=L−1K_n = \frac{2n}{n+1} - 1 = \frac{n-1}{n+1} \to 1 = L - 1Kn​=n+12n​−1=n+1n−1​→1=L−1 — K100=99101≈0.9802K_{100} = \frac{99}{101} \approx 0.9802K100​=10199​≈0.9802 matches the caption.

As a corollary of Gauss's test: for a>0a > 0a>0 and an=n!(a+1)(a+2)⋯(a+n)a_n = \frac{n!}{(a+1)(a+2)\cdots(a+n)}an​=(a+1)(a+2)⋯(a+n)n!​, show anan+1=1+an+O(1n2)\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} = 1 + \frac{a}{n} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)an+1​an​​=1+na​+O(n21​) (i.e. Gauss h=ah = ah=a), then prove via Kummer's test that ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ converges for a=2a = 2a=2 and diverges for a=12a = \frac12a=21​.

(The restriction a>0a > 0a>0 is needed: a=−1a = -1a=−1 makes a denominator 000 at n=1n = 1n=1, and a≤−1a \le -1a≤−1 can make factors 000 or negative, violating Kummer's hypothesis an>0a_n > 0an​>0.)

Show proof

  1. Computing the ratio directly: anan+1=n!(a+1)⋯(a+n)⋅(a+1)⋯(a+n+1)(n+1)!=n+a+1n+1=1+an+1\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} = \frac{n!}{(a+1)\cdots(a+n)} \cdot \frac{(a+1)\cdots(a+n+1)}{(n+1)!} = \frac{n+a+1}{n+1} = 1 + \frac{a}{n+1}an+1​an​​=(a+1)⋯(a+n)n!​⋅(n+1)!(a+1)⋯(a+n+1)​=n+1n+a+1​=1+n+1a​.

    Since an+1=an⋅nn+1=an−an(n+1)\frac{a}{n+1} = \frac{a}{n} \cdot \frac{n}{n+1} = \frac{a}{n} - \frac{a}{n(n+1)}n+1a​=na​⋅n+1n​=na​−n(n+1)a​, this is the Gauss form 1+hn+O(1n2)1 + \frac{h}{n} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)1+nh​+O(n21​) with h=ah = ah=a.

    And an+1→0\frac{a}{n+1} \to 0n+1a​→0, so the ratio tends to 111: the ratio test is powerless.

For a=2a = 2a=2 we verify the closed form: an=n!3⋅4⋯(n+2)=n!⋅2(n+2)!=2(n+1)(n+2)a_n = \frac{n!}{3 \cdot 4 \cdots (n+2)} = \frac{n! \cdot 2}{(n+2)!} = \frac{2}{(n+1)(n+2)}an​=3⋅4⋯(n+2)n!​=(n+2)!n!⋅2​=(n+1)(n+2)2​ (multiplying top and bottom by 1⋅2=21 \cdot 2 = 21⋅2=2 completes (n+2)!(n+2)!(n+2)!). Indeed a1=13=22⋅3a_1 = \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{2\cdot 3}a1​=31​=2⋅32​.

    So an=2(1n+1−1n+2)a_n = 2\left(\frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+2}\right)an​=2(n+11​−n+21​) telescopes: ∑n=1Man=2(12−1M+2)→1\sum_{n=1}^{M} a_n = 2\left(\frac12 - \frac{1}{M+2}\right) \to 1∑n=1M​an​=2(21​−M+21​)→1 — the series sums to 111.

For a=2a = 2a=2, Kn=n−1n+1→1>0K_n = \frac{n-1}{n+1} \to 1 > 0Kn​=n+1n−1​→1>0 (with Kn≥12K_n \ge \frac12Kn​≥21​ for n≥3n \ge 3n≥3), so Kummer's convergent half gives convergence — agreeing with the telescoping closed form (K100=99101≈0.9802K_{100} = \frac{99}{101} \approx 0.9802K100​=10199​≈0.9802).

Since ∑1pn=∑1n\sum \frac{1}{p_n} = \sum \frac{1}{n}∑pn​1​=∑n1​ diverges, Kummer's divergent half gives divergence of ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ (K1=−0.75K_1 = -0.75K1​=−0.75, K100=−51101≈−0.505K_{100} = \frac{-51}{101} \approx -0.505K100​=101−51​≈−0.505 — matching the caption).
